blocks.title: 1. Domain, Range, and the Vertical Line Test
teacherCues: Ask: 'Given a graph, how can we find all possible inputs and outputs?'
Use the Vertical Line Test to quickly check if a graph represents a function.

discoveryHook.scenario: A seismograph records ground motion during an earthquake. The wiggly line must pass the [[kw:Vertical Line Test]] because at any instant in time, there's only one shaking intensity. The set of times recorded is the [[kw:domain]]; the range of intensities is the [[kw:range]]. Graphs let us see these at a glance.

explanation: The [[kw:domain]] of a function shown by a graph is the set of all $ x $‑values for which there is a point on the graph. Look left and right.
The [[kw:range]] is the set of all $ y $‑values for which there is a point on the graph. Look down and up.
Closed dots mean points included; open dots mean excluded.
The [[kw:Vertical Line Test]]: If any vertical line intersects the graph in more than one point, the graph does NOT represent a function.
[[imp: A function has exactly one $ y $ for each $ x $; the Vertical Line Test checks this visually.]]

visuals.title: Interpreting Graph Features (like Figure 1.32)

rows.1: All $ x $-values from leftmost to rightmost point
All $ y $-values from lowest to highest point
Graph touches a vertical line twice

visuals.caption: A quick check: draw vertical lines; if any hit twice, it's not a function.

examples.title: A – Find domain and range from a graph
examples.prompt: A graph has points from $ x = -3 $ to $ x = 4 $, with a closed dot at $ (-3, -2) $ and an open dot at $ (4, 1) $. The lowest $ y $ is $ -2 $ and the highest $ y $ is $ 3 $. Find domain and range.
steps: Domain: $ x $ from $ -3 $ to $ 4 $, open at $ 4 $ → $ [-3, 4) $.
Range: $ y $ from $ -2 $ to $ 3 $, both endpoints closed → $ [-2, 3] $.

examples.title: B – Why the Vertical Line Test works
examples.prompt: Explain why the Vertical Line Test checks exactly the definition of a function.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about what a vertical line represents.
steps: A vertical line represents a specific $ x $ value.
If that line hits the graph more than once, that $ x $ has multiple $ y $ values.
This violates the rule that each input must have exactly one output.

examples.title: C – Apply the Vertical Line Test
examples.prompt: Does a circle centered at the origin represent $ y $ as a function of $ x $? (Think of drawing vertical lines.)
steps: Draw vertical lines through the circle; most will hit the top and bottom.
One $ x $ value gives two $ y $ values → fails the Vertical Line Test.
Therefore, a circle does NOT represent a function.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Passing the Vertical Line Test means it's a function, but the inverse may not be true. [[imp: A horizontal line can cross a function many times; that's fine.]]

questions.prompt: The Vertical Line Test says a graph is a function if every vertical line intersects it at most ___ point(s).
A graph has $ x $-values from $ -5 $ to $ 3 $ (both closed). Domain? (use interval notation)
If a graph has an open dot at the rightmost point $ (6,4) $, is $ 6 $ in the domain? (yes or no)

challengeCorner.prompt: A graph has domain $ (-\infty, \infty) $ but is only drawn above $ y=0 $. The range appears to be $ [0, \infty) $. Could this be the graph of $ y = x^2 $? Explain.
answers: x^2 is a function, domain all reals, range [0,∞)
hints: Check Vertical Line Test: $ y=x^2 $ passes.

blocks.title: 2. Zeros of a Function
teacherCues: Ask: 'Where does the graph cross the $ x $-axis?'
Explain that zeros are $ x $-values where $ f(x) = 0 $.

discoveryHook.scenario: A company's profit function $ P(x) $ has zeros where profit is zero—the break‑even points. The zeros of $ f(x) = 3x^2 + x - 10 $ are found by solving $ 3x^2 + x - 10 = 0 $. These $ x $-values are the $ x $-intercepts of the graph.

explanation: The [[kw:zeros]] of a function $ f $ are the values of $ x $ for which $ f(x) = 0 $.
Graphically, zeros are the $ x $-intercepts of the graph.
To find zeros algebraically: set the function equal to zero and solve for $ x $ (factor, square root, or multiply by denominator for rational functions).
[[imp: A function can have no zeros, one zero, or many zeros.]]

visuals.title: Finding Zeros – Examples
visuals.caption: Different function types require different solving techniques.

formulaCard.title: Finding Zeros
notes: For polynomials: factor, use quadratic formula, or square roots.
For rationals: set numerator = 0, exclude denominator = 0.
For radicals: isolate radical, square both sides, check for extraneous solutions.

examples.title: A – Find zeros of a polynomial
steps: Zeros: $ x = \frac{1}{2} $ and $ x = -3 $.

examples.title: B – Why set numerator=0 for rational functions?
examples.prompt: For $ h(x) = \frac{2x-3}{x+5} $, explain why we set $ 2x-3=0 $ to find the zero, but must check that $ x+5 \neq 0 $.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about what makes a fraction zero.
steps: A fraction equals zero when its numerator is zero (and denominator not zero).
We set $ 2x-3=0 $ to get $ x = 1.5 $, which doesn't make denominator zero.
Always ensure the denominator isn't zero at that $ x $; otherwise it's not in the domain.

examples.title: C – Square root function zero
steps: Square both sides: $ x-4 = 4 $ → $ x = 8 $.
Check: $ \sqrt{8-4} - 2 = 2-2 = 0 $, valid. Zero at $ x = 8 $.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: When solving radical equations by squaring, you might get extraneous solutions. [[imp: Always check the solutions in the original equation.]]

questions.prompt: The zeros of a function are the $ x $‑values where $ f(x) = $ ___.
Find the zeros of $ f(x) = x^2 - 9 $. (list numbers separated by comma)
What is the zero of $ g(x) = \frac{x-4}{x+1} $? (number only)

challengeCorner.prompt: Find the zeros of $ f(x) = \frac{x^2-1}{x-1} $. Note any domain restrictions.
hints: But $ x=1 $ makes denominator zero, so only $ x=-1 $.

blocks.title: 3. Increasing, Decreasing, and Constant Functions
teacherCues: Ask: 'As we move from left to right, when does the graph go up? Down? Stay flat?'
Show a graph and trace with finger.

discoveryHook.scenario: A stock price chart shows price going up in the morning, steady at lunch, then falling in the afternoon. These behaviors correspond to intervals where the function is [[kw:increasing]], [[kw:constant]], or [[kw:decreasing]]. Mathematical analysis of these intervals helps investors decide when to buy or sell.

explanation: A function $ f $ is [[kw:increasing]] on an interval if, as $ x $ increases, $ f(x) $ rises.
It is [[kw:decreasing]] if as $ x $ increases, $ f(x) $ falls.
It is [[kw:constant]] if $ f(x) $ stays the same throughout the interval.
To find these intervals, observe the graph from left to right and note where it goes up, down, or flattens.
[[imp: Increasing/decreasing is always stated over open intervals (in terms of $ x $).]]

visuals.title: Behavior from Graph (like Figure 1.36)
visuals.caption: Trace the curve with your finger: uphill = increasing; downhill = decreasing; flat = constant.

examples.title: A – Determine intervals from a described graph
examples.prompt: A graph falls from $ x=-3 $ to $ x=1 $, then rises from $ x=1 $ to $ x=4 $. Identify intervals of increase and decrease.
steps: Decreasing: $ (-3, 1) $.
Increasing: $ (1, 4) $.
No constant interval.

examples.title: B – Why open intervals?
examples.prompt: Explain why we typically use open intervals (parentheses) when describing where a function is increasing or decreasing, even if the behavior includes endpoints.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about what happens exactly at the turning point.
steps: At a turning point, the function is neither increasing nor decreasing for that instant.
Open intervals exclude the point itself, avoiding ambiguity.
It's a convention to make the description precise.

examples.title: C – Classify behavior from values
examples.prompt: For $ f(x) = x^3 $, as $ x $ goes from $ -\infty $ to $ \infty $, is $ f(x) $ ever constant? Is it increasing everywhere?
steps: $ f(x) = x^3 $ is not constant anywhere.
For any $ x_1 < x_2 $, $ x_1^3 < x_2^3 $, so it is increasing on $ (-\infty, \infty) $.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don't confuse 'positive' with 'increasing.' A function can have positive values but be decreasing (going down from a high positive to a lower positive). [[imp: Increasing/decreasing describes direction, not sign.]]

questions.prompt: If a graph goes down as $ x $ moves to the right, the function is ___.
From a graph, the function rises on $ (-\infty, 2) $ and falls on $ (2, \infty) $. At $ x = 2 $, is the function increasing? (yes or no)
hints: At the peak, it changes direction.

questions.prompt: A flat horizontal segment on a graph indicates the function is ___ on that interval.

challengeCorner.prompt: The function $ f(x) = |x| $ decreases on $ (-\infty, 0) $ and increases on $ (0, \infty) $. Where is the minimum value, and what is its type?
hints: The lowest point is at the vertex.
It's the absolute minimum and also a relative minimum.

blocks.title: 4. Relative Minima and Maxima
teacherCues: Ask: 'Where are the peaks and valleys of the graph?'

discoveryHook.scenario: A mountain range has local peaks (relative maxima) and valleys (relative minima). The highest peak is the absolute maximum, but each hilltop is a relative maximum. In math, we find these turning points to understand a function's shape.

explanation: A [[kw:relative maximum]] is a point where the function changes from increasing to decreasing; it is higher than nearby points.
A [[kw:relative minimum]] is a point where the function changes from decreasing to increasing; it is lower than nearby points.
A function can have multiple relative maxima and minima, but no more than one absolute maximum or minimum on a closed interval.
Approximating these points can be done with a graphing utility or by observing the graph.
[[imp: Relative extrema are $ y $-values, but we often refer to the point $ (x, y) $ as the extremum.]]

visuals.title: Identifying Extrema from Graph

rows.2: Constant on one side, falls on other

visuals.caption: Peaks are maxima; valleys are minima; plateaus are typically not extrema.

formulaCard.title: Relative Extrema
formulaCard.formula: $$ f(a) \text{ is a relative min if } f(a) \le f(x) \text{ nearby} $$ $$ f(a) \text{ is a relative max if } f(a) \ge f(x) \text{ nearby} $$
notes: Use a graphing utility to approximate; precalculus methods provide exact values later.
Extrema are $ y $-values; the $ x $-value is where they occur.

examples.title: A – Approximate a relative minimum
examples.prompt: Graph $ f(x) = 3x^2 - 4x - 2 $ on a calculator. Zoom in to find the approximate relative minimum point.
steps: The graph is a parabola opening upward; vertex is the minimum.
Using trace or minimum feature: $ x \approx 0.67 $, $ y \approx -3.33 $.
Relative minimum is about $ -3.33 $ at $ x \approx 0.67 $.

examples.title: B – Distinguish relative from absolute extrema
examples.prompt: Explain the difference between a relative maximum and an absolute maximum.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about a function that oscillates.
steps: A relative maximum is the highest point in a local neighborhood; there can be many.
The absolute maximum is the highest point over the entire domain; at most one.
Example: $ y = \sin x $ has many relative maxima (1), but no absolute max because it's periodic.

examples.title: C – Identify extrema from description
examples.prompt: A graph increases to $ (3, 7) $, then decreases, then increases again from $ (5, 1) $. Identify the relative extrema.
steps: $ (3, 7) $ is a relative maximum (peak).
$ (5, 1) $ is a relative minimum (valley).
There are no other extrema described.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Endpoints of a domain can be absolute extrema, but they are not relative extrema (by definition). [[imp: Relative extrema require an interval on both sides.]]

questions.prompt: A relative minimum occurs where a function changes from decreasing to ___.
Is the point $ (0,0) $ a relative minimum of $ f(x) = x^2 $? (yes or no)
hints: It's the lowest point of the parabola.

questions.prompt: A function has a peak at $ x = 2 $ where $ f(2) = 5 $. This is a relative ___ (minimum or maximum).

challengeCorner.prompt: Use a graphing utility to approximate the relative maximum of $ f(x) = -4x^2 - 7x + 3 $.
hints: The vertex of a downward parabola is the maximum.

blocks.title: 5. Even and Odd Functions
teacherCues: Ask: 'What kind of symmetry does $ y = x^2 $ have? What about $ y = x^3 $?'
Define even and odd functions in terms of $ f(-x) $.

discoveryHook.scenario: The graph of $ f(x) = x^2 $ is a mirror across the $ y $-axis—the left side is a reflection of the right. Such functions are called [[kw:even functions]]. $ f(x) = x^3 $ looks the same after a 180° rotation about the origin—these are [[kw:odd functions]]. Recognizing these symmetries simplifies graphing.

explanation: A function is [[kw:even]] if $ f(-x) = f(x) $ for all $ x $ in the domain. Graph is symmetric about the $ y $-axis.
A function is [[kw:odd]] if $ f(-x) = -f(x) $ for all $ x $ in the domain. Graph is symmetric about the origin.
To test algebraically, compute $ f(-x) $ and compare to $ f(x) $ and $ -f(x) $.
A function can be neither even nor odd.
[[imp: Even functions have only even powers (after simplification); odd functions have only odd powers.]]

formulaCard.title: Even and Odd Functions
notes: For even functions, the graph is symmetric about the $ y $-axis.
For odd functions, the graph is symmetric about the origin.

examples.title: A – Test for even/odd
examples.prompt: Determine if $ g(x) = x^4 - 2x^2 $ is even, odd, or neither.
steps: Since $ g(-x) = g(x) $, $ g $ is even.

examples.title: B – Why $ f(-x) = -f(x) $ means odd
examples.prompt: Explain why the condition $ f(-x) = -f(x) $ implies the graph is symmetric about the origin.
examples.peerPrompt: Consider a point $ (a, b) $ on the graph. Where is $ (-a, -b) $?
steps: If $ (a, b) $ is on the graph, $ b = f(a) $.
For odd function, $ f(-a) = -f(a) = -b $, so $ (-a, -b) $ is also on the graph.
The two points are symmetric about the origin (180° rotation).

examples.title: C – Classify a function
examples.prompt: Is $ h(x) = \frac{1}{x} $ even, odd, or neither? (Assume $ x \neq 0 $.)
steps: Therefore, $ h $ is odd.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The exponents alone do not guarantee even/odd if there are constants or absolute values. [[imp: Always test algebraically with $ f(-x) $.]]

questions.prompt: A function is even if $ f(-x) = $ ___.
Is $ f(x) = |x| $ even, odd, or neither?
If $ g $ is odd and $ g(2) = 5 $, what is $ g(-2) $? (number only)

challengeCorner.prompt: A function $ f $ is defined by $ f(x) = 3x^5 - 2x^3 + x $. Prove that $ f $ is odd.
